overview: This file documents wartime mobilization and military-security measures in Japanese colonial Taiwan during March 1938, amid the Second Sino-Japanese War (“China Incident”). American Consul Gerald Warner reports a press-driven counterespionage campaign, the compulsory drilling and ideological assimilation of Taiwanese Chinese adults, a public funeral for Japanese soldiers killed in China, and daily military-aircraft exercises over Taipei. An enclosed newspaper translation describes the organization, membership, reporting rules, and propaganda activities of spy-prevention societies across Taiwan and the Penghu Islands. A final State Department memorandum considers whether the reported aviation activity might constitute an impermissible strengthening of coastal defenses under Article 19 of the Washington Naval Treaty.

subfiles.title: Despatch from Gerald Warner on military and wartime activities in Taiwan
subfiles.from: Gerald Warner, American Consul at Taihoku
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports counterespionage agitation, compulsory civilian drills, a military funeral, and aircraft maneuvers in colonial Taiwan during March 1938.
subfiles.summary: Warner identifies the expanding newspaper campaign and formation of local spy-prevention societies as the month's most important development, noting that suspicion of Chinese residents and foreigners was obstructing the consulate's contacts and commercial investigations. He reports that approximately 15,000 Taiwanese Chinese men and an equal number of women underwent compulsory drills in Taipei on March 19–24 as part of spiritual mobilization and imperial-assimilation efforts. He also describes the March 26 municipal funeral for four Japanese soldiers killed in China and daily mock-combat exercises by eight biplanes over Taipei.

subfiles.title: Taiwan Shimbun translation on island-wide spy-prevention societies
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, as an enclosure to Gerald Warner's despatch
subfiles.about: Describes the organization and activities of spy-prevention bodies in Keelung, Tainan, Penghu, Datun, Beidou, and other Taiwanese localities.
subfiles.summary: The article describes Keelung's plan for an integrated citywide surveillance network divided between Japanese ward societies and Taiwanese Chinese volunteer-police societies, operating in liaison with military authorities. It reproduces substantial portions of the Tainan society's bylaws, which require reporting suspicious foreigners, photography or surveying near military sites, and inquiries into strategic industries and natural resources. A six-hour conference at Magong brought together civil, police, military, and naval officials for lectures on military secrecy, national defense, and espionage methods. Shorter notices describe organizing efforts in Datun and Beidou and note similar societies in Changhua, Yuanlin, and Yilan, while observing that none had yet been formed in Taipei.

subfiles.title: State Department memorandum on air forces and Article 19 of the Washington Treaty
subfiles.from: S. R., Division of Western European Affairs
subfiles.to: E. E. D., apparently in Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Considers whether the reported military aviation activity in Taiwan violated treaty restrictions on strengthening coastal defenses.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum concludes that the action reported from Taihoku would not appear to contravene Article 19 of the Washington Treaty unless the buildup and strengthening of air forces were treated as an increase in coastal defenses. It raises a comparative question about whether the United States had itself increased its air forces in its Pacific possessions since 1922.

interest: The file offers an unusually detailed view of how counterespionage was turned into a mass civic obligation in colonial Taiwan, including the actual reporting categories, institutional membership, ethnic separation, and military-police liaison proposed for local societies. Warner's comments also reveal the immediate effect of this atmosphere on foreign consular work and interpersonal contacts. The juxtaposition of colonial mobilization, public ritual, aviation exercises, and Washington treaty analysis makes the bundle particularly useful for studying the intersection of surveillance, imperial assimilation, military preparedness, and international law on the eve of the Pacific War.
